Pea Coat
PEE koht
noun (Navy)
The Oxford English Dictionary gives it as a compound of English pea and coat, with its earliest evidence in 1790, in the Pennsylvania Packet. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains pea from “pilot cloth,” sometimes called P-cloth, which made a “p-jacket” and later a pea coat; NHHC dates the term to 1723, earlier than the OED’s first evidence. The two accounts differ.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A pea coat is the heavy topcoat worn by seafaring men in cold, miserable weather. NHHC says the name does not come from pea-soup weather. The coat was once tailored from pilot cloth, a heavy, coarse, stout twilled blue cloth with the nap on one side; the cloth was sometimes called P-cloth from its initial letter, the garment a p-jacket, and later a pea coat. The OED’s earliest record is 1790. The Christian observation: warm clothing against the cold is a mark of good provision in Scripture. The virtuous woman “is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet” (Pro 31:21). Paul, in prison and near the end, asked Timothy to bring “The cloke that I left at Troas” (2Ti 4:13). And Job counted it righteousness that he had not “seen any perish for want of clothing” (Job 31:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

A sailor’s heavy cold-weather topcoat (OED earliest 1790); NHHC derives it from pilot cloth or P-cloth. A household clothed against the snow (Pro 31:21).

PEA COAT (also peacoat), n. (from 1790, OED) A heavy topcoat worn by sailors in cold weather. Compound of pea and coat (OED).

Origin note: NHHC derives pea from pilot cloth, called P-cloth, and dates the term to 1723.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:21 — "She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet."

2Ti 4:13 — "The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments."

Job 31:19 — "If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering;"

Modern Corruption

A pea coat is plain provision against the weather; the error is to treat clothing as display instead of covering, and to forget the poor who have none.

expand to see more

The pea coat has been adopted ashore as fashion, and there is no harm in a good coat. But Scripture’s interest in clothing is covering and provision. The household clothed in scarlet is warm (Pro 31:21), and Paul wanted his cloak because the prison was cold (2Ti 4:13).

Job’s test is the one that matters: did anyone perish for want of clothing while he had it to give (Job 31:19)? A Christian’s wardrobe is measured by what it covers, including what it gives away.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

pea + coat (OED earliest 1790). NHHC: pilot cloth → P-cloth → p-jacket → pea coat (NHHC date 1723).
